props.title: Shoeshine
props.initialSlug: Two shoeshine boys' friendship tested by crime & betrayal

sections.content: Shoeshine (1946) marks a defining moment in Italian Neorealism, capturing post-WWII Italy's devastated social fabric through the eyes of two young shoeshine boys. Director Vittorio De Sica crafts a heartbreaking portrait of childhood friendship destroyed by poverty and systemic corruption. The film's raw emotional power influenced later youth-focused dramas like Los Olvidados (1950) and Pixote (1981), establishing a template for depicting children struggling against societal forces beyond their control. De Sica's documentary-style approach, using non-professional actors and real locations, became a hallmark of neorealist cinema.

sections.content: The influence of Shoeshine extends far beyond Italian cinema. Its unflinching look at institutional cruelty toward children echoes in films like The 400 Blows (1959) and Salaam Bombay! (1988). De Sica's technique of following children through harsh urban environments created a visual language adopted by filmmakers worldwide, from Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali (1955) to Héctor Babenco's Pixote (1981).

The film's prison sequences revolutionized how youth incarceration was depicted on screen. Its influence can be traced through Bad Boys (1983), Starred Up (2013), and Capernaum (2018). De Sica's decision to show the brutal reality of juvenile detention challenged censorship standards and opened the door for more honest portrayals of youth in crisis. sections.content: Shoeshine helped establish social realism as a global film movement. Its DNA can be found in British kitchen sink dramas like Kes (1969), Indian parallel cinema such as Ankur (1974), and contemporary works like Fish Tank (2009). The film's influence on depicting youth alienation and institutional failure remains powerful in works like the Dardenne brothers' La Promesse (1996) and Rosetta (1999).
